Optimization and Control.summary: We study accelerated proximal gradient methods with general stepsizes for convex composite multiobjective optimization, in which every objective is the sum of a smooth convex term and a proper closed convex extended-valued term, and the proximal subproblem retains a separate offset for each objective. The momentum coefficient may depend on the computed trajectory. For a two-parameter root momentum rule we prove boundedness, weighted square summability of the displacements, a merit-function rate of $o(k^{-2})$, and displacement decay of $o(k^{-1})$ whenever the first parameter converges to a value in $(0,1)$; the second parameter need not converge or have bounded total variation. The analysis is organized as a chain of basic estimates, an energy identity, coefficient asymptotics, and auxiliary lemmas that are reused in every regime. For the critical parameter $α=3$ we establish the finite bound $u_0(x^N)\le 2\ell R/[N(N+3)]$, square summability of the displacements, displacement decay $O(1/N)$, and convergence of the full sequence to a weak Pareto point. The remaining little-o question at $α=3$ is shown to be exactly the vanishing of a nonnegative critical energy, so it is separated from the large-$O$ estimate rather than left as a missing step. For $1<α<3$ we give the rate $O(N^{-(α-1)})$ and for every $α>0$ the qualitative conclusion $u_0(x^k)\to0$, $F_i(x^k)\to c_i$, and $\sum_k D_k/k<\infty$. A table summarizes the rate picture over the whole positive range of $α$, and a JOS1 experiment illustrates the predicted little-$o$ separation.

Optimization and Control.title: Attraction-Ranking Mismatch in Out-of-Distribution Detection: Theory and Evidence from Hamiltonian Feature Dynamics
Optimization and Control.summary: Attracting features toward learned in-distribution (ID) regions is an intuitive strategy for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, but does such attraction improve detection? We investigate this question using class-conditioned Hamiltonian dynamics as a controlled testbed and identify an attraction-ranking mismatch: improving individual class-affinity scores need not improve the relative ordering of ID and OOD samples. Our analysis separates misalignment between the driving field and the detection score from ranking failure that persists even when they are aligned. An exact AUROC decomposition and a local boundary analysis identify relative score changes at the ID-OOD ranking boundary as the source of first-order AUROC change under regularity conditions. Experiments demonstrate that a score-aligned rule can improve performance on a held-out source validation split yet consistently degrade it after transfer, even without a single winning-class change. A separate perturbation study finds that near-boundary relative score changes track the direction of small AUROC changes in the tested settings. Finally, centroid approximation and shared scales connect the zero-step score to a static centroid family that includes the existing CTM detector. Together, these results explain why class attraction is insufficient to justify feature refinement and motivate evaluating its effect on the ranking boundary.

Optimization and Control.title: An exact column generation algorithm for load balancing in capacity sharing networks
Optimization and Control.summary: Capacity sharing networks are typical heterogeneous communication networks widely applied in information and communications technology (ICT) field. In such networks, resources like bandwidth, spectrum, computation and storage are shared among various communication services. Meanwhile, the issue of network congestion is always a prominent challenge. To handle network congestion essentially needs to solve the load balancing of networks. In this paper, for capacity sharing networks, we formulate their load balancing problem as a maximum multi-commodity flow problem. For such a problem, always a large-scale linear programming, the column generation algorithm is a commonly used and crucial method to solve it. In each iteration, this algorithm involves solving a linear programming subproblem and determining whether to terminate or generate a new column for inclusion in the subproblem. This iterative procedure of solving and checking continues throughout the algorithm. Nevertheless, since the checking subproblem is NP-hard, its solution significantly impacts the overall efficiency of the algorithm. In this paper, we innovatively convert the checking subproblem into a single-constrained shortest path (SCSP) subproblem. By exactly solving the SCSP subproblem, we can obtain the optimal solution to the checking subproblem with same or less computing time. Experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm achieves computational efficiency comparable to heuristic algorithms while outperforming other state-of-the-art algorithms by at least an order of magnitude.

Optimization and Control.title: Infinite-Time Mean Field FBSDEs and the Associated Elliptic Master Equations
Optimization and Control.summary: We study discounted infinite-time mean field forward-backward stochastic differential equations (FBSDEs) and the associated elliptic master equations, which were introduced in [20] as mathematical tools for solving discounted infinite-time mean field games. We first establish stability and flow properties, identify the backward decoupling field with the spatial derivative of the equilibrium value function, and prove that the value function is a viscosity solution of the master equation. Under additional smoothness and quantitative stability assumptions, we construct its Lions-derivative and the required higher-order derivatives using variational results from a companion paper [21]. These results show that the value function is a classical solution of the elliptic master equation. We also prove that the value function is the unique displacement-monotone regular solution.

Optimization and Control.title: Fréchet Regression on the Bures-Wasserstein Manifold
Optimization and Control.summary: Fréchet regression, or conditional Barycenters, is a flexible framework for modeling relationships between covariates (usually Euclidean) and response variables on general metric spaces, e.g., probability distributions or positive definite matrices. However, in contrast to classical barycenter problems, computing conditional counterparts in many non-Euclidean spaces remains an open challenge, as they yield non-convex optimization problems with an affine structure. In this work, we study the existence and computation of conditional barycenters, specifically in the space of positive-definite matrices with the Bures-Wasserstein metric. We provide a sufficient condition for the existence of a minimizer of the conditional barycenter problem that characterizes the regression range of extrapolation. Moreover, we further characterize the optimization landscape, proving that under this condition, the objective is free of local maxima. Additionally, we develop a projection-free and provably correct algorithm for the approximate computation of first-order stationary points. Finally, we provide a stochastic reformulation that enables the use of off-the-shelf stochastic Riemannian optimization methods for large-scale setups. Numerical experiments validate the performance of the proposed methods on regression problems of real-world biological networks and on large-scale synthetic Diffusion Tensor Imaging problems.

Optimization and Control.title: BFGS can converge to non-Clarke-stationary points with positive probability
Optimization and Control.summary: We construct a coercive, locally Lipschitz, semialgebraic function on $\mathbb R^2$ for which BFGS with Armijo--Wolfe line search converges to a non-Clarke-stationary point from a nonempty open set of initial points and inverse-Hessian estimates. This disproves the almost-sure stationarity assertion in the 2013 challenge of Lewis and Overton. The construction and proof combine analytical arguments with computer-assisted verification of explicit inequalities.

Optimization and Control.title: Weak and strong convergence of a general splitting approach for monotone multioperator inclusions
Optimization and Control.summary: In this paper, we study a general forward-backward splitting approach for monotone inclusion problems that simultaneously accommodate set-valued, monotone Lipschitz continuous, and cocoercive operators. Weak convergence is established under a general setting. Strong convergence is obtained when both the maximally monotone operators are linear relations and the monotone Lipschitz continuous and cocoercive operators are linear. When the set-valued operators are normal cones to closed linear subspaces, we derive an explicit characterization of limit points of generated sequences using a new technique. Numerical experiments on a quadratic minimization problem with multiple-set split feasibility constraints are presented to illustrate the theoretical results.

Optimization and Control.title: On Convergence of Gradient Temporal-Difference Learning with Regularized Corrections and Eligibility Traces
Optimization and Control.summary: Temporal-difference (TD) learning underlies many prediction and control algorithms, but can diverge when combined with off-policy learning, bootstrapping, and function approximation. TD with Regularized Corrections (TDRC) is theoretically sound and practically simple, but existing convergence theory covers only the one-step case under i.i.d. sampling, while the Huber Bellman-error formulation has not been extended to TDRC or eligibility traces. In this work, we establish convergence of constrained TDRC($λ$) with diminishing stepsizes and non-i.i.d. off-policy data, for state-dependent and history-dependent $λ$-parameters. We also propose TDRC($λ$)-Huber, which preserves the TDRC($λ$) fixed point while reducing sensitivity to large Bellman errors. For both algorithms, we apply an ODE-based weak-convergence method from stochastic approximation theory. For the nonlinear mean dynamics of TDRC($λ$)-Huber, we give an integral small-gain condition that guarantees uniqueness and global asymptotic stability of the target equilibrium. We then establish convergence of the constrained algorithm, derive computable sufficient conditions for convergence, and identify a regularization-based convergence mechanism shared by linear TDRC($λ$) and TDRC($λ$)-Huber. When the mean TD matrix is positive stable, both constrained algorithms converge under sufficiently strong regularization without requiring positive definiteness.
Optimization and Control.comment: 66 pages, 1 figure. Submitted to the Journal of Machine Learning Research

Optimization and Control.title: On-Line Policy Iteration with Trajectory-Driven Policy Generation
Optimization and Control.summary: We consider deterministic finite-horizon optimal control problems with a fixed initial state. We introduce an on-line policy iteration method, which, starting from a given policy, however obtained, generates a sequence of cost-improving policies and corresponding trajectories. Each policy produces a trajectory, which is used in turn to generate data for training the next policy. The method is motivated by problems that are repeatedly solved starting from the same initial state, including discrete optimization and path planning for repetitive tasks. For such problems, the method is fast enough to be used on-line. Under a natural consistency condition, we show that the sequence of costs of the generated policies is monotonically improving for the given initial state (but not necessarily for other states). We illustrate our results with computational studies from combinatorial optimization and 3-dimensional path planning for drones and a robot arm in the presence of obstacles. We also discuss briefly a stochastic counterpart of our algorithm. Our proposed framework combines elements of rollout and policy iteration with flexible trajectory-based policy representations, and applies to problems involving a single as well as multiple decision makers. It also provides a principled way to train neural network-based policies using trajectory data, while preserving monotonic cost improvement.

Optimization and Control.title: Effect of a fourth-order diffusion term on the robustness of the transfer function stability for hyperbolic systems
Optimization and Control.summary: We study a $2\times2$ hyperbolic system with anti-located control and observation. It is well known that the system can be stabilized with a delayed output-feedback control and that, unfortunately, this design is arbitrarily sensitive to small errors in the transport velocity. It was recently proved that adding a second-order diffusion term to the system restores robustness. We show that the same phenomenon occurs with a fourth-order diffusion term: the maximal spectral abscissa of the closed-loop system converges, as the diffusion parameter goes to zero, to the explicit value $-\ln(2)$, and the resulting stability margin is robust to small perturbations of the transport velocity. This additional term leads to a quartic characteristic equation whose roots have no tractable closed-form expression. We develop an asymptotic classification of its four roots and use it to obtain a first-order expansion of the transfer function with an explicit error bound. Combining this expansion with a topological degree argument, we show that $-\ln(2)$ is in fact the exact limiting value of the spectral abscissa, extending to the fourth-order case the sharpness result previously available only for second-order diffusive terms.

Optimization and Control.title: Pathwise-Budgeted LLM Routing: Online Allocation with K-Bit Tail-Cost Learning
Optimization and Control.summary: Firms using large language models under fixed budgets must decide which model to call and whether to retry a failed task. Because a call's charge is revealed only after completion, one long response can exhaust the remaining budget and leave later tasks unserved. Our objective is to maximize the number of tasks solved before service stops. We develop a contextual bandit policy, ADP-HT, which learns each model's task-specific success probability and constructs conservative cost estimates from coarsened response-length labels on a quantile grid with $2^K$ intervals. The policy weighs predicted success against these costs, adjusting the cost penalty to realized spending and the budget available per remaining task. Under calibration, local regularity, and grid-coverage conditions, we bound the excess allowance in the policy's conservative cost estimates. At a fixed sample size, increasing $K$ reduces the discretization term but increases the estimation allowance. At the tightest tested budgets, ADP-HT solves more than twice as many MATH500 and GPQA tasks as the best implemented baseline. It achieves the highest mean cumulative score at ten of fourteen RouterBench budgets. On LiveCodeBench, it outperforms a deployed commercial router in both default and cost-saving modes at the three lowest test budgets.

Optimization and Control.title: Observability and stabilizability for Grushin-Type parabolic equations in the whole space
Optimization and Control.summary:
We study observability and stabilization for the whole-space Grushin heat equation $$ \partial_t u-Δ_γu=0,\qquad Δ_γ:=Δ_x+|x|^{2γ}Δ_y,\qquad (t,x,y)\in(0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m,\quad γ>0. $$ For product sets $E=E_1\times E_2$, we identify three observability regimes in which thickness, distance from the degeneracy set $\{x=0\}$, and local density near that set play different roles.
  (i) In the subcritical regime $0<γ<1$, the observability inequality holds for every $T>0$ if and only if both $E_1$ and $E_2$ are thick; hence $T_{\min}(E)=0$.
  (ii) At the critical exponent $γ=1$, if $E_2=\mathbb{R}^m$ and $E_1\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ is thick, we determine the exact minimal observable time: $$ T_{\min}(E)=\frac{a_{\mathrm{ess}}(E_1)^2}{2n},\qquad a_{\mathrm{ess}}(E_1):=\operatorname*{ess\,inf}_{x\in E_1}|x|. $$ Thus, the threshold depends on the essential distance of $E_1$ from the degeneracy set.
  (iii) In the supercritical regime $γ>1$, we consider $n=1$, $E_2=\mathbb{R}^m$ and thick sets $E_1\subset\mathbb{R}$. If $a_{\mathrm{ess}}(E_1)>0$, observability fails for every $T>0$, so that $T_{\min}(E)=+\infty$. If $a_{\mathrm{ess}}(E_1)=0$, observability depends on the density of $E_1$ near $0$, measured by $$ D_{E_1}(r):=\log\!\left(\frac{2r}{|E_1\cap(-r,r)|}\right),\qquad L_{E_1}:=\limsup_{r\downarrow0}r^2D_{E_1}(r). $$ If $L_{E_1}=0$, then $T_{\min}(E)=0$; if $0<L_{E_1}<\infty$, a finite sufficient observation time exists. Moreover, observability at time $T$ requires $$ \limsup_{r\downarrow0}r^{2(1+γ)/(γ-1)}D_{E_1}(r)\le C_{T,γ}. $$
  In contrast, for every $γ>0$, exponential and complete stabilizability hold if and only if both $E_1$ and $E_2$ are thick. The stabilization criterion is therefore independent of $γ$.

Optimization and Control.title: Analysis of a Two Membrane Thermoelastic Problem
Optimization and Control.summary: We formulate and study a mathematical model of a thermoforming process involving two interdependent thermoelastic membranes coupled with equations governing heat transfer. These membranes interact with each other through means of elastic forces and thermal transfer which determines changes in elastic properties and further deform the membranes. The two thermoelastic membranes lead to a pair of implicit obstacle problems which are modeled both as a 2-membrane problem or a pair of quasi-variational inequalities. Mathematically, the primary model couples an elliptic two membrane problem with associated nonlinear elliptic equations describing temperature distribution. We show, under physically relevant conditions, the existence of solutions via a fixed point approach that involves reformulation of the problem to improve regularity of solutions.

Optimization and Control.title: Near-Optimal Complexity of Finding Approximate Local Minima of Nonconvex Finite Sums
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the component-oracle complexity of finding approximate local minima of nonconvex finite sums under mean-squared averaged smoothness with parameter $L$ and a $ρ$-Lipschitz average Hessian. Each query returns the value, gradient, and one Hessian-vector product of a component. We show that the complexity in the high-accuracy regime $\varepsilon\le c_0L^2/(nρ)$ is $\tildeΘ(n^{3/4}L^{1/2}ρ^{1/4}Δ\varepsilon^{-7/4})$ for a sufficiently large initial gap $Δ$. We attain the upper bound by adapting the inverse solver and eigenvector routine of FastCubic to averaged smoothness. Our lower bound assigns the bridge edges of a nested chain to random components; a replicated spectral construction gives the same bound for unrestricted randomized algorithms. Under individual smoothness, a factor of $n^{1/4}$ remains for $\varepsilon\le cL^2/(n^2ρ)$, up to logarithmic factors. In the complementary low-accuracy regime, we propose PathVR, which uses $\tilde O(n+\sqrt{n}LΔ\varepsilon^{-2})$ queries and matches a lower bound from dense weak hiding.

Optimization and Control.title: Variable Bound Tightening for Nash Equilibrium Computation in Multiplayer Imperfect-Information Games
Optimization and Control.summary: There has been significant recent progress in algorithms for approximation of Nash equilibrium in large two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games and exact computation of Nash equilibrium in multiplayer strategic-form games. While counterfactual regret minimization and fictitious play are scalable to large games and have convergence guarantees in two-player zero-sum games, they do not guarantee convergence to Nash equilibrium in multiplayer games. Recently, an approach has been presented for exact computation of Nash equilibrium in multiplayer imperfect-information games that solves a quadratically constrained program based on a nonlinear complementarity problem formulation derived from the sequence-form game representation. This formulation was solved using Gurobi's nonconvex quadratic solver, which employs spatial branch-and-bound to iteratively refine variable bounds by solving convex relaxations of bilinear terms. During presolve, Gurobi introduces auxiliary variables and, in some cases, binary variables, leading to an internal mixed-integer quadratically constrained program. This approach was demonstrated to outperform prior algorithms from the Gambit software suite and quickly solve three-player Kuhn poker after removal of dominated actions; however, the algorithm was not able to solve the full version of the game within 24 hours. In this paper, we derive finite bounds on slack and multiplier variables in the nonlinear complementarity formulation. These bounds can strengthen the convex relaxations used within spatial branch-and-bound. We compare uniform corollary bounds with finer proposition-based bounds on full three-player Kuhn poker. All eight bounded configurations return numerically verified equilibria in under 17 seconds, while the unbounded formulation finds no feasible solution within 300 seconds. The finest bounds do not consistently yield the fastest computation.

Optimization and Control.title: Bilevel Learning via Strategically Inexact Stochastic Gradient Descent
Optimization and Control.summary: Bilevel optimization is a central tool in computational imaging for high-dimensional hyperparameter tuning; prominent applications include learning data-adaptive regularizers and optimizing forward operators in variational regularization. However, due to the nested nature of the problem, exact gradients with respect to the parameters (so-called hypergradients) are not available: the precision of the hypergradient is linearly related to the computational cost, thus requiring algorithms which can solve the problem without unnecessary precision. In learned-regularizer pipelines, the inner reconstruction solver is typically run for a fixed number of iterations, leaving the hypergradient accuracy uncontrolled and existing convergence theory inapplicable. In this work, we analyze the schedules that practitioners actually run: we prove convergence of inexact stochastic bilevel optimization and establish rates under both decaying accuracy and step size schedules, showing that, with optimal configurations, convergence occurs at an $O(k^{-1/4})$ rate in expectation. This is the optimal rate of nonconvex stochastic gradient descent and matches single-loop stochastic bilevel methods; with warm-started inner solves, total costs also agree up to constants. Experiments on image denoising and inpainting with convex ridge regularizers and input-convex neural networks confirm our analysis: decreasing step sizes improve stability, accuracy scheduling is more critical than step size strategy, and adaptive preconditioning (e.g., Adam) further boosts performance, particularly for input-convex neural networks. In a budget-matched comparison with four state-of-the-art single-loop methods, accuracy-scheduled stochastic gradient descent and its Adam variant attain the highest test peak signal-to-noise ratio.
Optimization and Control.comment: 10 pages + 6 pages supplementary material. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Computational Imaging

Optimization and Control.title: Conditions for Normality of Pontryagin's Maximum Principle in the Absence of State Constraints
Optimization and Control.summary: Pontryagin's Maximum Principle is said to be "normal" for the problem at hand when it has a solution (maximizer u*) that explicitly involves the problem's cost function, making the maximum principle helpful (while in the opposite situation it is of no help). The aim of the present paper is, for Lagrange optimal control problems without state constraints, to identify classes of problems for which the Principle is normal. General conditions are introduced that guarantee normality, and classes of problems that satisfy these conditions are identified. Such classes include problems for which the constrained (by bounds on the control values) "augmented" reachable set, with cost along an upward vertical axis, has a convex lower-boundary function and the optimal terminal state lies in the relative interior of the reachable state set, with the terminal constraint within the affine hull of that set. Such classes include problems for which the constrained (by bounds on the values of the control signal) "augmented" (with the cost value along an upward "vertical axis") reachable set has a "convex" lower boundary for which the optimal terminal state lies in the relative interior of the set of reachable states. Special attention is given to Lagrange steering problems: sufficient conditions are obtained on a nested sequence of sub-classes of such problems, culminating with the class of steering problems with scalar control signal and linear time-invariant (LTI) state dynamics and objective integrand, for which normality is guaranteed whenever all eigenvalues of the state dynamics matrix A are real (e.g., if A is symmetric or triangular or the system is overdamped) or have small enough imaginary parts; simple 2 x 2 examples show that, in contrast with the situation in the finite-dimensional case, this property does not extend to arbitrary A matrices.

Optimization and Control.title: Translate, then decide: asymptotic optimality of latent-space control in bistable systems
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper asks whether an optimal decision can be separated from the physical dynamics on which it acts. It studies this question through minimum-energy barrier crossing in scalar bistable systems. It characterizes the finite-horizon optimal feedback and shows that, as the horizon grows, it converges to a law that doubles and reverses the drift while it opposes crossing, and switches off once the barrier is passed. In physical coordinates, this law inherits the plant's nonlinearity, entangling decision and dynamics. We show that a plant-specific translation of state, input, and time maps every double well in the considered class to the same unit-rate linear world model, allowing a downstream decision stage to use a single plant-independent control primitive. This separation generally loses optimality at finite horizons because the translation does not preserve the physical control energy. Nevertheless, we prove that the excess physical energy of the layered controller vanishes as the horizon grows and that its limiting feedback reproduces the asymptotic optimum exactly. Thus, translation and optimization generally do not commute at a finite horizon, but commute in the asymptotic limit.

Optimization and Control.title: Mixed-Integer Second-Order Cone Formulations for the Euclidean Bottleneck Steiner Tree Problem in $\mathbb{R}^d$
Optimization and Control.summary: Given a set of terminals in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and an integer $k\ge0$, the Euclidean bottleneck Steiner tree problem (EBSTP) asks for a tree spanning the terminals with at most $k$ Steiner points that minimizes its longest edge. Although the planar case has been widely studied, exact optimization methods for arbitrary dimension remain scarce. We develop two exact mixed-integer second-order cone programming (MISOCP) formulations for the EBSTP: a single-commodity flow formulation and a formulation with connectivity cuts. Both formulations share a geometric core based on edge-conditional second-order cone constraints and are strengthened by problem-specific preprocessing, edge-dependent big-$M$ constants, symmetry-breaking constraints, constructive upper bounds, and new global lower bounds on the optimal value. We establish the correctness of the formulations and prove the validity of all strengthening techniques. Computational experiments on 1050 benchmark instances in dimensions $d\in\{2,3,4\}$, with up to $50$ terminals and $9$ Steiner points, show that the single-commodity flow formulation consistently outperforms the formulation with connectivity cuts, with an advantage { in solved instances} that grows with dimension. The proposed global lower bounds substantially strengthen the root relaxation, while the single-commodity flow formulation provides the most robust exact solution method across all test sets. These results establish the single-commodity flow formulation as an effective exact approach for the EBSTP in arbitrary fixed dimension.

Optimization and Control.title: Do Language Models Know Which Constraints Belong Together?
Optimization and Control.summary: Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation strengthens the linear relaxation of a mixed-integer program by convexifying a chosen set of constraint families, and every candidate costs a column generation run. The choice is hard when families strengthen the bound only together, because a search that adds one family at a time then stops at the linear relaxation. The classical inequalities of lot sizing, network design and facility location rest on such zero-marginal groups. We prove that when each evaluation convexifies at most $s$ of $k$ families, any method that observes only bounds needs a covering number of evaluations, of order $k^w$, to find a hidden group of $w$ families, also on actual Dantzig-Wolfe relaxations. A prediction that misses $e$ members reduces the cost to $Θ(k^e)$, through one staged search that does not need to know $e$, so the evaluations a prediction saves measure what the predictor knows. We study two sources of predictions. A one-pass lookahead at an optimal LP dual is provably blind to groups whose families share no variable, and a language model reads the names and text of the model. JointDW verifies the prediction of the language model with the staged search and interleaves it with the lookahead at a bounded loss. Groups that strengthen the bound only jointly appear in a quarter of the MIPLIB-NL models whose bound can be improved. There the strongest language models identify them about as often as the lookahead, their predictions rest on the names for textbook models, and reasoning about doubles the accuracy of the same model. On larger models with distracting families, the lookahead finds the group in one evaluation of three families. Language models given only the text seldom name it, while one reasoning model given every coefficient names it in all but one answer and then needs fewer evaluations than the lookahead for pairs of families.
Optimization and Control.comment: 23 pages, 4 figures, 15 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/junbolian/JointDW

Optimization and Control.title: Recovery Theory for Projected Power Iterations in Permutation Synchronization
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the projected power method for permutation synchronization: recovering $n$ unknown permutations of $m$ objects from pairwise relative permutations, observed independently with probability $p$ and independently corrupted by uniform permutations with probability $1-π_0$. Our main theorem establishes uniform one-step contraction for all estimates with optimally aligned block-error fraction at most $1/2-ε$, for fixed $ε>0$, including measurement-dependent estimates. When $np\ge C_0\log(n)$ and $m=o(npπ_0^2)$, one update contracts the error by a factor $O(m/(npπ_0^2))$, up to a floor of $O(e^{-c\min\{m\,npπ_0^2,\,npπ_0\}} + \log(n) / n)$. Thus, every initialization in this majority basin achieves $o(1)$ error after one update and maintains it uniformly over subsequent iterations. A reference-block spectral initializer enters the basin with probability $1-o(1)$, yielding end-to-end almost-exact recovery. If additionally $\min\{m\,npπ_0^2,\,npπ_0\} \ge C\log(n)$ for sufficiently large $C$, the method achieves exact recovery in finitely many iterations. We also establish prescribed-block recovery under weaker conditions for measurement-independent estimates and extend the guarantees to independent permutation-valued corruptions with uniform mean and to partial permutations with common visible support.

Optimization and Control.title: Efficient Receding Horizon Control for Stabilizing 2D Navier--Stokes Flows with Finitely Many Localized Actuators and POD Acceleration
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper develops and analyzes a computationally efficient receding horizon control (RHC) strategy for steering two-dimensional Navier--Stokes flows to prescribed reference trajectories. The control is represented by a finite linear combination of localized actuators supported within a prescribed control subdomain. At the continuous PDE level, we establish local exponential stabilization in the $L^2$-norm and suboptimality of the actuator-based RHC scheme for weak solutions. Direct implementation requires the repeated solution of high-dimensional finite-horizon optimal control problems. To reduce this computational cost, we combine RHC with model order reduction based on proper orthogonal decomposition (POD). A common POD space constructed from state snapshots reduces the state and adjoint equations and accelerates the online optimization, while the resulting controls are applied to the full-order discretized dynamics. Numerical experiments for two flow configurations of increasing complexity examine the influence of actuator layouts, prediction horizons, viscosity, and POD dimension. The numerical results demonstrate substantial reductions in computational cost while maintaining closed-loop stabilization in the tested configurations.

Optimization and Control.title: Relevance Propagation as Entropic Optimal Transport on Filippov Neural Networks: Sinkhorn Propagation and Region Relevance in Image Classifiers
Optimization and Control.summary: Relevance propagation, which redistributes a network's prediction backward through the layers, is usually treated as a heuristic. We show that it is the solution of a single variational problem: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) is the divergence-free flow on the active computational graph of zero relative entropy to the backward transition law of the forward activation flow; for a non-negative reference, this is a relative entropy between Markov measures on backward paths. The rules LRP$_0$, LRP$_{z^+}$ and LRP$_{α,β}$ follow from this principle by the choice of a reference, and are instances of one rule, LRPN$_{α,β}$, whose weights may vary from node to node, for instance with the node's activity, in the spirit of Hebb's principle. The principle rests on a measure-theoretic formalization of feed-forward networks as directed acyclic graphs of Filippov operators, which covers piecewise-smooth and discontinuous architectures (e.g. hard-routed Mixture-of-Experts) with a Clarke-Filippov generalized-gradient calculus; it also characterizes backpropagation as the adjoint equation of a Lagrangian relaxation. On networks of ReLU and max-pooling nodes, LRP$_0$ is Gradient$\times$Input, with an explicit jump across a kink where LRP$_{z^+}$ stays continuous. Taking the entropy edge by edge yields a new rule, Sinkhorn Relevance Propagation. Aggregated over an input region, the flow of a non-negative reference tells, with exact accounting, which hidden units carry its evidence, the conditioned flow being a Schrödinger bridge. On VGG-16, the conservation identities hold to round-off, and the rules are told apart by the sign of their maps, the share of the output left to the bias nodes, faithfulness, localization and class dependence; on ConvNeXt-Tiny, LRPN$_{α,β}$ conserves the output and its Hebbian weights give the highest ABPC of the rules tested.

Optimization and Control.title: Universal Adaptive Proximal Gradient Methods via Gradient Mapping Accumulation
Optimization and Control.summary: We propose an adaptive proximal gradient method for minimizing the sum of two functions, where one is a simple convex function, and the other belongs to one of the three classes: nonconvex smooth, convex nonsmooth, or convex smooth. The key feature of the method is an adaptive step size that accumulates historical gradient mapping norms in the denominator. Without any modification or knowledge of problem parameters, the method converges across all three problem classes under mild bounded-iterates and bounded-variance assumptions, with rates matching those of the proximal gradient method up to logarithmic factors, in both deterministic and stochastic settings. For the convex setting, we further propose an accelerated variant. It retains a similar near-optimal convergence rate for the nonsmooth case and achieves an improved rate of order $\widetilde{O}\big(1/t^2 + σ/\sqrt{t}\big)$ for the smooth case, which is optimal up to logarithmic factors. Notably, we develop new techniques for controlling the effect of stochastic noise, which are applicable across all three problem classes in the stochastic setting and enable a simplified analysis.

Optimization and Control.title: Tight Lower Bounds under Matched High-Order Hölder Smoothness and Uniform Convexity
Optimization and Control.summary: In this paper, we provide tight lower bounds for minimizing high-order Hölder-smooth and uniformly convex functions when their orders match. Specifically, we consider functions whose $p^{th}$-order derivatives are Hölder continuous with degree $ν$ and parameter $H$, and that are uniformly convex with degree $q$ and parameter $σ$. When these orders match, namely, $q = p + ν$, we show that any deterministic algorithm with access to derivatives up to order $p$ requires $Ω\left(\left(\frac{H}σ\right)^{\frac{2}{3(p+ν)-2}}\log\frac{Δ_0}ε\right)$ oracle calls to reduce an initial optimality gap of $Δ_0$ to $ε$. This matches the corresponding upper bound and establishes a higher-order uniformly convex counterpart to Nesterov's classical first-order lower bound for strongly convex functions. Rather than directly generalizing Nesterov's classical quadratic-chain construction, we develop a multiscale phase-wise construction that preserves previous oracle responses while maintaining global Hölder smoothness and uniform convexity. Our result resolves the matched case left open by existing lower bounds for the two asymmetric regimes.

Optimization and Control.title: Generalized Disjunctive Programming with Derivative-Free Configuration Search
Optimization and Control.summary: Generalized disjunctive programming (GDP) describes process design alternatives with Boolean variables, disjunctions, and logical propositions, and fixing one configuration leaves a subproblem in the continuous variables. Conventional GDP methods require explicit equations, which a simulator may not expose, and mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) reformulations can be intractable for nonconvex models. The external-variable reformulation turns configuration choice into an optimization over an integer lattice whose objective is the subproblem value, which derivative-free optimization (DFO) can search while the GDP model continues describing the alternatives. We pair GDP models with surrogate DFO methods and the direct-search method NOMAD and compare them with discrete steepest descent (D-SDA), logic-based and MINLP solvers, and enumeration on nine process models, 21 test functions, a pharmaceutical flowsheet simulated in PharmaPy, and a catalytic distillation column with 100,947 configurations. On the largest reactor network, the surrogate methods MISO and RBFOpt reach the reference in nine or ten of ten runs with about 30 subproblem solves, whereas logic-based methods solve nearly one subproblem for each admissible configuration and most D-SDA descents end at one local minimum. In the flowsheet example, where GDP solvers do not apply, RBFOpt and MISO find the best of 36 simulated configurations in every run with 20 evaluations. For the catalytic column, D-SDA and MISO reach the best known design with 100 evaluations, whereas MINLP solvers find no design within 15% of it and global solvers return contradictory certificates. This search pays off when the configuration space is too large to enumerate, has deceptive local minima, or has MINLP reformulations that fail, and enumeration or a direct reformulation is simpler for small algebraic models.

Optimization and Control.title: Designing an Adaptive Robust and Evolutionary-Game Framework for Minimum Shipment Quotas in Capacity-Constrained Freight Markets
Optimization and Control.summary: Minimum shipment quota regulations ensure that socially critical commodities are not excluded from capacity-constrained freight markets by profit-driven allocation. Existing models of such regulation are deterministic and static, assuming perfect market knowledge and instantaneous convergence to a rational equilibrium. This paper relaxes both assumptions through a framework combining adaptive robust optimization, multi-objective optimization, and evolutionary game theory. A robust optimization model first characterizes the regulator's quota-setting problem under uncertain commodity availability, trading social welfare against enforcement cost to generate a Pareto frontier of quota policies. This frontier then defines the regulator's strategy space in a three-population evolutionary game in which the regulator, suppliers, and carrier co-evolve under replicator dynamics, so that the prevailing policy emerges from the interaction of the three players. The framework is calibrated to a Canadian rail freight case study that covers crude oil, corn, barley, and oat. Quota regulation raises social welfare from 65.0 to 288.2 million CAD, at an enforcement cost of about 2% of the gain. Two findings carry particular policy weight: capacity shortfalls fall entirely on unprotected commodities the carrier ships voluntarily, sparing both the highest-margin and the protected products; and a fall in transport cost can end the regulation while the exclusion it was designed to correct persists, because the margin observable before bidding diverges from the margin prevailing once suppliers adapt.

Optimization and Control.title: Common Noise by Random Measures: Constructing Mean-Field Equilibria for Competitive Investment and Hedging
Optimization and Control.summary: We construct Nash equilibria in mean-field portfolio games of optimal investment and hedging under relative performance concerns with exponential (CARA) utility preferences. Common noise dynamics are modeled by integer-valued random measures, for instance Poisson random measures, in addition to Brownian motions. Agents differ in individual risk aversions, competition weights, and initial capital endowments, while their contingent claim liabilities depend on both common and idiosyncratic risk factors. Mean-field equilibria are characterized by solutions to McKean-Vlasov backward stochastic differential equations with jumps, for which we prove existence and uniqueness of solutions, without assuming mean-field interaction to be small. Moreover, we show how the equilibrium can be constructed from the optimal strategy of a single-agent optimization problem (without mean-field interaction) via an appropriate projection. Using successive changes of measure, our derivation provides a decomposition of the equilibrium strategy into three components with clear interpretations. Finally, we show how a limiting mean-field game of quadratic (instead of utility-based) hedging with relative performance concerns arises for vanishing risk aversion.
Optimization and Control.comment: Improved exposition. The first version (arXiv:2408.01175v1) of this preprint has been published under the slightly different title "Common Noise by Random Measures: Mean-Field Equilibria for Competitive Investment and Hedging''; subsequent versions (with the new title) feature several new results relative to v1

Optimization and Control.title: A simple adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging method for unconstrained convex optimization in $p$-norm geometry
Optimization and Control.summary: Efficient preconditioning plays an important role in large-scale first-order optimization. In this paper, we propose an adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging ($\text{A}^2$ODA) method for unconstrained convex optimization that adopts low-cost preconditioning based on $p$-norm geometry for $p\in[2,\infty]$. The method is line-search-free and employs a new stepsize selection technique based on an aggregated affine lower model. Its update structure is simple and unified across $p\in[2,\infty]$, with the case $p>2$ requiring no more elaborate updates than the Euclidean case $p=2$. Under a generalized local smoothness condition, we derive a convergence bound that separates the effects of constant and gap-dependent curvature, with the latter potentially yielding faster-decaying terms. In the special case of local smoothness, this bound recovers a nearly optimal convergence rate.

Optimization and Control.title: Quantification of Tail-trimming Effects for Interval CVaR Based Nonlinear Regression
Optimization and Control.summary: The tail trimming strategy is widely adopted for robustness against outlier contamination in statistical learning and operations research. However, it generally lacks the thorough understanding that to what extent the tail-trimming technique is effective for nonlinear regression. In this paper, we address the robust nonlinear regression based on the so-called interval conditional value-at-risk (In-CVaR), which is introduced to guard against outliers by trimming extreme losses. We first analyze the trimming effect of the In-CVaR based estimator under distributional perturbation. Our first finding is that the In-CVaR based estimator is qualitatively robust under distributional perturbation in terms of the Prokhorov metric if and only if the largest portion of losses is trimmed. Furthermore, under sample contamination, we derive a probably approximately correct (PAC) bound for the In-CVaR based estimator, showing that the preliminary covariate filtering that is customary in the literature is not needed for In-CVaR based regression. The nonconvexity of the In-CVaR objective, together with unboundedness of covariates, responses and parameter space create the technical challenges for our developed theory, and thus necessitate the new treatment of the qualitative robustness and PAC analysis. Overall, this study rigorously analyzes robustness properties of In-CVaR based nonlinear regression models, which illustrates to what extent the right tail-trimming of the loss by In-CVaR risk measure is essential and effective for robust nonlinear regression. These theoretical findings are further supported by numerical experiments.

Optimization and Control.title: A Fully Polynomial Approximation Algorithm for the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick Model
Optimization and Control.summary: Montanari's incremental approximate message passing (IAMP) algorithm [FOCS 2019; SIAM J. Comput., 2025] and the zero-temperature formulation of El Alaoui, Montanari and Sellke (AMS) [Ann. Probab., 2021] find a $(1-\varepsilon)$ approximation to the maximum Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) energy in $C(\varepsilon)N^2$ operations for fixed accuracy, with probability tending to one as $N\to\infty$, under their respective full-support and access-model assumptions. However, it was unknown whether this approximation could be achieved with work polynomial in both $N$ and $1/\varepsilon$, together with quantitative guarantees at finite dimension. Under the same assumptions as AMS, we introduce grouped IAMP with exact Gaussian query outputs (GEG-IAMP), which is the first SK approximation algorithm with total work polynomial in $N$ and $1/\varepsilon$ and a finite-size guarantee above a dimension threshold polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$ and $\log(1/α)$. More precisely, for every $α\in(0,1/2)$, it returns a $(1-\varepsilon)$ approximation with probability at least $1-α$ whenever $N\ge \mathsf{K}\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2(e/\varepsilon)\log(\mathsf{K}/α)$, using $O(N^2/\varepsilon)$ work and $O(N^2)$ storage. GEG-IAMP replaces the Onsager correction by Reeves's coupling construction [arXiv:2508.10782] and groups Euler-Maruyama steps into $O(1/\varepsilon)$ matrix-vector products. We also prove a relative guarantee for AMS IAMP with $O(N^2\varepsilon^{-3}\log^2(e/\varepsilon))$ work but a sufficient dimension exponential in inverse accuracy. By returning a fixed configuration below its dimension threshold, GEG-IAMP also provides an asymptotic fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme (AFPRAS), with an additive error independent of dimension.

Optimization and Control.title: Logarithmic Regret for Alternating Mirror Descent
Optimization and Control.summary: Alternating online mirror descent (AltOMD) is a simple learning rule for zero-sum games, which improves upon simultaneous OMD numerically and theoretically. Previous work obtained $O(T^{1/3})$ and $O(T^{1/5})$ regret bounds for AltOMD, by leveraging modified-energy-function-based analyses. However, settling whether AltOMD achieves near-constant regret has remained an open question. In this paper we resolve the question of whether AltOMD achieves near-constant regret in the affirmative. In particular, we show an $O(log(T))$ regret bound on the sum of the players' external regrets for any two-player zero-sum bilinear game with compact convex strategy sets, under mild regularity assumptions on the regularizers. We verify that our assumptions hold for the negative entropy regularizer, thereby obtaining logarithmic regret for the alternating multiplicative weights updates algorithm. The regret bound also yields an $O(log(T)/T)$ duality gap bound for the averaged strategies.

Optimization and Control.title: Accelerated Concatenation of Stepsize Schedules for Smooth Strongly Convex Gradient Descent
Optimization and Control.summary: This work considers stepsize schedules for gradient descent on smooth strongly convex objectives. We develop a curvature-dependent concatenation framework for constructing stepsize schedules of arbitrary length with sharp worst-case guarantees. Within this framework, we introduce two families of schedules for the function-value gap and gradient norm of the last iterate, respectively. For each fixed condition number $κ=L/μ>1$, both families attain iteration complexity $Θ(κ^ρ\log(1/ε))$ for sufficiently small $ε$, where $ρ=\log_{\sqrt2+1}2\approx0.7864$. This complexity is optimal up to a subpolynomial factor in $κ$ among predetermined nonnegative stepsize schedules. The framework also recovers the strongly convex silver schedule at power-of-two iteration budgets and applies to smooth convex and smooth weakly convex functions.

Optimization and Control.title: Handling Customer Preferences in Last-Mile Location-Routing: A Bilevel Optimization Approach
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper introduces the Location-Routing Problem with Delivery Preferences, a last-mile delivery problem with service flexibility that integrates collection-point activation and routing decisions while accounting for customer choice. The company determines which collection points to activate, which customers to offer home delivery, and the corresponding delivery route. Customers subsequently decide whether to accept the proposed home-delivery service or collect their parcels from an activated collection point according to ranked preferences over delivery time intervals and collection points. This hierarchical interaction is modeled through a bilevel optimization framework, which can be formulated as a mixed-integer bilevel program that incorporates compensation mechanisms for service inconvenience. Two equivalent single-level reformulations that exploit the structure of the customers' problems are developed. In addition, a two-phase heuristic is proposed to generate feasible solutions that can be used as warm starts for the formulations. The computational experiments run to compare the performance of the formulations, show that the warm-start strategy becomes particularly effective as the instance size increases. The comparison with a benchmark model that ignores customer preferences indicates that explicitly accounting for customer choice alters the resulting location-routing configuration while improving customer preference satisfaction at a small increase in the company's overall cost. These findings highlight the importance of jointly considering operational efficiency, service flexibility, and customer autonomy in last-mile delivery planning.

Optimization and Control.title: Converses of Moreau's decomposition theorem
Optimization and Control.summary: We study when generalized metric projections generated by strongly quasiconvex functions are polarizable. The point of departure is Moreau's decomposition theorem, where the Euclidean metric projections onto two mutually polar closed convex cones form complementary retractions whose sum is the identity. This suggests the following fundamental question: when does a given retraction admit such a complementary polar retraction? We formulate this notion through polarizable retractions and then specialize it to generalized projections of the form $x\mapsto P_{\cal C}^\varphi(x)$, defined by minimizing $\varphi(x-y)$ with respect to $y$ over a closed convex set ${\cal C}$. After recalling basic properties of mutually polar retractions and first-order characterizations of generalized projections, we prove the main result: If $\varphi$ is strongly quasiconvex, the generalized projection $P_{\cal C}^\varphi$ is polarizable if and only if ${\cal C}$ is a closed convex cone. Thus, polarizability of the projection is characterized by the conic geometry of its range. Hence, this result can be considered as a converse of Moreau's decomposition theorem. As a consequence, a more specific converse of the same theorem is presented for the Euclidean norm.

Optimization and Control.title: A Minimax Analysis of the Last Iterate of the SubGradient Method in Finite Dimension
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the last iterate of the projected subGradient Method with a constant stepsize for convex $L$-Lipschitz objectives in $\mathbb{R}^d$, minimized over closed convex sets. Assuming that the initial iterate $x_1$ has distance at most $R$ from a minimizer, we establish matching upper and lower bounds on the minimax optimization error at $x_n$, where the infimum is taken over constant stepsizes. Specifically, this error is of order $L\cdot R\cdot\sqrt{\min\{d,\log n\}/n}$. Notably, when the dimension is fixed, the minimax error decays as $1/\sqrt{n}$, without the extra logarithmic factor intrinsic to dimension-free analyses. Our analysis exploits a combinatorial argument based on linear algebra and novel geometric constructions.
Optimization and Control.comment: 25 pages, 2 figures. Substantially revised and expanded; sharp minimax bounds after optimizing over constant stepsizes. Title and abstract updated

Optimization and Control.title: Minimal Reflected BSDEs and Superhedging of Irregular American Claims
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the superhedging of American claims with an irregular optional payoff process $ξ$ over the full set $\mathcal{M}(X)$ of equivalent local martingale measures of a locally bounded market. We show that a process which is a strong optional supermartingale of class (D) under every $Q\in\mathcal{M}(X)$, with no bound from either side, decomposes as $S=S_0+\int H\,dX-A-C_-$, with a common integrand $H$, a right-continuous increasing process $A$ and a purely discontinuous increasing process $C$ given explicitly by the right jumps of $S$. For the robust Snell envelope this yields the superhedging duality $p_0(ξ)=\sup_{Q}\sup_τE^Q[ξ_τ]$ with an explicit optimal strategy and no regularity of $ξ$ in time. Unbounded payoffs are covered when $\{ξ_τ\}$ is uniformly integrable jointly over measures and stopping times, or when $|ξ|$ is dominated by a traded uniformly integrable martingale. For payoffs bounded below, the price is attained by wealth bounded below by a constant. For payoffs unbounded below this can fail, already in a complete market, and the price is attained once the constant bound is replaced by $-M$, with $M$ a traded martingale dominating $|ξ|$. In an incomplete Brownian market we study the associated reflected BSDE with an optional obstacle and a Lipschitz driver depending on the value. We prove existence and uniqueness of the minimal supersolution, a representation at stopping times, comparison and an equivalent dynamic minimality condition, for bounded data and for data dominated by a traded martingale. For a European-type obstacle, the Skorokhod conditions on the total regulator hold for some supersolution if and only if the terminal claim is attainable by a bounded wealth process; so in an incomplete market some data admit no supersolution satisfying them, while the right-jump regulator always satisfies its contact condition.

Optimization and Control.title: Riemannian EXTRA: Communication-efficient decentralized optimization over compact submanifolds with data heterogeneity
Optimization and Control.summary: We consider decentralized optimization over a compact Riemannian submanifold in a network of $n$ nodes, where each node $i$ owns a smooth nonconvex local objective $f_i$ defined by its private data, and the goal is to minimize the global objective $F(x)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)$ using only local communications. A naive Riemannian extension of EXTRA leaves the auxiliary normal-space error uncontrolled and does not inherit the Euclidean convergence guarantees. We develop projection-based Riemannian EXTRA (REXTRA) and a retraction-based counterpart that incorporate a normal correction into both the communicated variable and the auxiliary update, while using only one local-variable-sized message per optimization iteration. By jointly controlling consensus, tangent, and normal errors, our analysis interprets the update as a network-based Riemannian inexact-gradient step. For projection-based REXTRA, a sufficiently small constant stepsize and a local initialization yield vanishing consensus, stationary accumulation points, and an $\mathcal O(1/k)$ best-iterate stationarity--consensus bound. For the retraction-based method, we prove that its difference from the projection update is uniformly second order and establish the same convergence properties and rate under a local initialization. Numerical experiments on representative manifold-valued learning tasks demonstrate the communication efficiency of the REXTRA updates.

Optimization and Control.title: Enabling risk and reliability analysis in next-generation computational tools via multifidelity methods
Optimization and Control.summary: Risk and reliability analysis are fundamental to the design, assessment, and operation of safety-critical complex systems; however, their integration into next-generation computational tools is constrained by the cost of uncertainty quantification with expensive computational models. The computational challenge is particularly prohibitive for tail-sensitive quantities, such as probabilities of failure, conditional values-at-risk, and buffered probabilities of failure, where accurate estimation can require a large number of model evaluations. Multifidelity methods provide a framework for addressing this computational bottleneck by combining information from models of varying accuracy and cost while retaining the predictive accuracy of the high-fidelity model. This review summarizes the state of the art in methods that enable scalable risk and reliability analysis using multifidelity control variates, multifidelity importance sampling, and multifidelity active learning.

Optimization and Control.title: Reformulation Techniques for PDLP with Applications to QUBO and Joint Replenishment
Optimization and Control.summary: Practitioners of linear programming widely believe that reformulating a linear program (LP) offers little benefit to interior-point methods: their iteration counts are famously insensitive to the formulation, so the payoff of reformulation beyond automatic presolve and customized linear solve is modest. This paper presents evidence that the same is not true of first-order solvers built on the primal-dual hybrid gradient method (PDHG), such as PDLP. Unlike interior-point methods, PDHG-type methods have per-iteration costs governed by the matrix representation of the formulation and iteration counts governed by its geometry, and both change under equivalent reformulations. We describe a general reformulation recipe: constraints drawn from a catalogue of projection-friendly polyhedra can be absorbed into the projection step of PDHG. We analyze what absorption does to the four constants that govern restarted PDHG: the coupling norm, the termination certificate, the distance scale, and the sharpness modulus. We perform the reformulation on two case studies. On the LP relaxation of quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO), absorption makes any step size below $1$ admissible on every instance, and yields a fully explicit linear rate. On the LP relaxation of the joint replenishment problem (JRP), whose optimum certifies a $2$-approximation for an NP-hard inventory problem, absorption improves the coupling norm and eliminates every matrix-vector product. Both reformulations run on GPUs with custom kernels in place of sparse matrix-vector products. We benchmark both against the GPU LP solver cuPDLPx applied to the original formulations. By solve time, the reformulated solvers are $6.4$-$9.6\times$ faster on QUBO and $6.1$-$28.9\times$ faster on the JRP. They take $1.7$-$4.3\times$ and $13.6$-$52.3\times$ fewer iterations respectively.

Optimization and Control.title: Variance Reduction Note 4: The Convergence of SVRG
Optimization and Control.summary: Stochastic variance-reduced gradient (SVRG) uses a full gradient at a snapshot point to correct inexpensive component gradients. This fourth expository note on variance reduction explains that control variate and gives a self-contained proof of linear convergence for the classical strongly convex finite-sum setting. Each component is assumed convex and smooth, while only their average must be strongly convex. A second-moment bound links the estimator to the objective gaps at the current iterate and the snapshot. Summing a distance recursion over an epoch then yields a geometric decrease and an oracle complexity of order $(n+L/μ)\log(1/τ)$ for objective accuracy $τ$, with the initial gap fixed. The result uses a random snapshot update and counts all full-gradient computations. No new algorithm or rate is claimed.

Optimization and Control.title: On the non-uniformity of the 2026 FIFA World Cup draw
Optimization and Control.summary: The group stage of a sports tournament is often made more appealing by introducing additional constraints in the group draw that promote an attractive and balanced group composition. For example, the number of intra-regional group matches is minimised in several world championships. Under such constraints, the traditional draw procedure may become non-uniform, meaning that the feasible allocations of the teams into groups are not equally likely to occur. Our paper quantifies this non-uniformity of the 2026 FIFA World Cup draw for the official draw procedure, as well as for 47 reasonable alternatives implied by all permutations of the four pots and two group labelling policies. We show why simulating with a recursive backtracking algorithm is intractable, and propose a workable implementation using integer programming. The official draw mechanism is found to be optimal based on two of five non-uniformity measures, including the average distortion of the 771 non-zero assignment probabilities. Nonetheless, non-uniformity can be more than halved if the organiser aims to treat the best teams drawn from the first pot equally.

Optimization and Control.title: Finite Spectral Depth Controls Gaussian Entrance Rank and Avoidance of the First Gradient-Flow Saddle
Optimization and Control.summary: Matrix factorization provides a simple model for studying the training dynamics of neural networks. Recent studies of gradient flow under small initialization have analyzed how trajectories escape from a neighborhood of the origin and approach their first nonzero stationary point. In this paper, we study continuous-time dynamics that applies a finite number of Newton-Schulz iterations to the normalized matrix gradient (Muon). We show that the number of Newton-Schulz steps can change the rank selected during the early stages of training and allow the resulting trajectory to bypass the first nonzero stationary point approached by gradient flow. Under an additional residual-inertia condition, we prove that bypass occurs for all sufficiently large finite Newton-Schulz depths and provide an explicit sufficient threshold. We also construct an example in which the bypass threshold is four.

Optimization and Control.title: Two-Player Zero-Sum Hybrid Games with Set-Valued Dynamics
Optimization and Control.summary: In this paper, we formulate a two-player zero-sum game under dynamic constraints defined in terms of a hybrid inclusion. The game consists of a min-max problem involving a cost functional that depends on the actions and corresponding (potentially non-unique) solutions, defined as functions of hybrid time and, hence, can flow or jump. We present sufficient conditions given in terms of Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs-like equations to establish a bound and to exactly evaluate the worst-case cost under the optimal strategy. Under additional conditions, we show that the proposed optimal state-feedback laws render a set of interest pre-asymptotically stable for the resulting hybrid closed-loop system. The results are illustrated in an application with sporadic jumps and linear quadratic hybrid dynamics.

Optimization and Control.title: Distributionally Robust Dynamic Inventory Control: Automatic Recovery under Martingale Demand
Optimization and Control.summary: Problem definition: We study dynamic inventory control for battery-swapping stations that combine central replenishment with automatic local recovery. Central replenishment improves immediate battery availability but reduces the depleted-battery pool available for subsequent recovery, creating an intertemporal trade-off. Managing this trade-off is particularly challenging when historical demand data are limited and future demand is uncertain and temporally dependent. Methodology/results: We develop a time-consistent distributionally robust dynamic program under martingale demand ambiguity, using the latest observed demand as the next conditional mean without requiring a fully specified demand distribution. We establish an optimal order-up-to policy for every finite horizon and identify two critical recovery rates governing replenishment decisions. Under a regular penalty condition, we derive explicit finite-horizon policies and worst-case demand distributions, showing that sufficiently strong automatic recovery makes central replenishment unnecessary in nonterminal periods. Extensions to submartingale and supermartingale demand reveal contrasting behaviors, including eventual full-capacity replenishment under upward ambiguity and recovery-induced positive replenishment under downward ambiguity. Managerial implications: Numerical experiments demonstrate that the robust policy is particularly competitive when demand is highly dispersed and historical information is limited, whereas its advantage diminishes when demand becomes more predictable or the conditional-mean assumption becomes less reliable. Our findings also reveal that greater reliance on local recovery may compromise service availability, highlighting the importance of jointly considering demand information, recovery capability, and service requirements when making replenishment decisions.

Optimization and Control.title: A constraint dissolving method for generally constrained optimization over a nonconvex set
Optimization and Control.summary: This manuscript studies a constraint dissolving method for solving optimization problems with general constraints, comprising an abstract constraint G(x) \in C and a potentially nonconvex geometric constraint x \in D, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first constraint dissolving type method applicable to this general setting. More specifically, we introduce an auxiliary variable s to decouple G(x) \in C into G(x) = s and s \in C, and construct the constraint dissolving mapping acting jointly on both variables. We then propose a penalty-based constraint dissolving method, in which the penalty parameter is updated adaptively according to the feasibility error. Under mild conditions, every accumulation point is Mordukhovich-stationary. By a specific choice of the constraint dissolving mapping, every accumulation point is guaranteed to be feasible, which stands in contrast to standard penalty-type methods in nonconvex settings. Numerical experiments on Rosenbrock, portfolio, and MAXCUT problems demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method against the augmented Lagrangian and the penalty decomposition methods.

Optimization and Control.title: LQG solution for POMDP without estimating states: A minimum variance approach
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper investigates the control of discrete-time linear time-invariant (LTI) systems subject to incomplete and corrupted measurements. Specifically, we focus on designing a Linear Quadratic Gaussian (LQG) controller without relying on explicit state estimation. By leveraging minimum variance duality, our approach allows the current control input to be represented as a linear function of available measurements and previously applied inputs, successfully reducing the task to a tractable deterministic optimization problem. We provide theoretical justification for this framework and demonstrate its practical effectiveness through numerical experiments.

Optimization and Control.title: Matching with Choice: Menu Design for Patient--Provider Assignment
Optimization and Control.summary: High-quality matches between patients and primary care providers improve downstream health outcomes, yet provider turnover breaks these matches and forces patients to be reassigned. Health systems facing this problem must decide not only which providers to recommend, but how much choice to offer. Direct assignment avoids competition for scarce provider capacity but relies on noisy estimates of patient preferences; broader choice allows patients to correct these estimates using private information but can create costly coordination failures. We study this tradeoff through the design of fixed, personalized menus from which patients choose providers. We show that constructing the optimal menu is NP-hard and establish an information-theoretic lower bound. We find that offering each patient a single provider matches this bound up to a constant factor, while unrestricted choice can perform arbitrarily poorly. However, we show that additional choice improves on single-provider assignment when the system cannot reliably distinguish among a patient's alternatives. We formalize this tradeoff through two forms of loss: menu loss, which arises when menus offer too few options, and coordination loss, which arises when scarce capacity is exposed to too much choice. Motivated by this decomposition, we develop the Scenario-Averaged Marginals (SAM) algorithm, which tailors menus based on provider shadow prices so choice is offered only when utility exceeds the capacity cost. We identify sufficient conditions which SAM's regret matches the lower bound, namely when patients have valuable alternatives and offered menus don't create competition for scarce capacity. In a semi-synthetic environment calibrated to a provider network using Medicare data, SAM improves total utility by up to 19% over single-provider assignment as preference uncertainty grows, while improving utility for the least-served ZIP codes.

Optimization and Control.title: Quadratic Returns for a Moving Water Tank: An Explicit Right Inverse and a Sylvester Representation
Optimization and Control.summary:
Coron's return method established local nonlinear controllability of a moving water tank in sufficiently large time. The quadratic response at uniform equilibrium is studied in this work, where the acceleration input in the linearized model cannot excite the Fourier modes of the fluid with even indices. At three one-way wave crossings ($T=3$), the quadratic final-state map on a family of delayed controls that return the linearized state to zero is reduced to a scalar expression associated with a planar curve. A constant-level curve gives the return, and a tangential variation yields an explicit right inverse of the derivative of the quadratic final-state map. This inverse acts on all missing modes and maps mean-zero periodic $H^r$ targets to $H^r$ controls for every nonnegative integer $r$. A contraction argument also gives local exact solvability of the quadratic final-state equation. Finally, a time-dependent Sylvester equation provides an alternative representation of the coupling responsible for the second-order correction. The associated change of state coordinates involves one spatial derivative, while the control correction preserves regularity in appropriate Sobolev spaces. These results concern the first two variation equations only, while nonlinear controllability at this time remains open.
  Keywords: Controllability, control of partial differential equations, return method, Saint-Venant equations, Sylvester equations.

Optimization and Control.title: How to Look Inside the Black Box: A Survey of Yu. E. Nesterov's Contributions (On the Award of the 2026 Gauss Prize)
Optimization and Control.summary: On July 23, 2026, at the opening of the International Congress of Mathematicians in Philadelphia, the International Mathematical Union announced the award of the Gauss Prize to Yurii Evgenievich Nesterov -- an award for mathematical work with significant applications outside mathematics. This article explains the mathematical content of the recognized work of Yu. E. Nesterov and traces its influence on modern computational practice. The exposition is based on a concept that Yu. E. Nesterov himself regards as one of his main results: the classical complexity theory of convex optimization is oriented toward a black-box oracle, but its pessimistic bounds can be overcome by using a priori information about the internal structure of the objective function. We trace Yu. E. Nesterov's scientific career, then introduce the language of oracle complexity together with a classification of objective function models (geometric, algebraic, and structural), and subsequently discuss his main results in chronological order: the fast gradient method, fast automatic differentiation, the theory of self-concordant barriers and polynomial-time interior-point methods, the $π/2$ theorem, the stable dynamics model of traffic flows, the smoothing technique, primal-dual methods, cubic regularization of Newton's method, the modified Gauss--Newton scheme, coordinate descent methods and methods for huge-scale problems, gradient-free methods, universal gradient methods, implementable tensor methods, and "superfast" methods. Each topic is accompanied by historical background, precise statements specifying the problem class, oracle, and type of guarantee, examples, and a discussion of the current state of the art.
Optimization and Control.comment: 115 pages, in English; 7 figures, 4 tables, 191 references

Optimization and Control.title: Asymptotic Optimality of $cμ$-Rule for LLM Inference Scheduling under Memory Constraint
Optimization and Control.summary: Large language model (LLM) inference, the process by which a pre-trained model receives an input prompt and generates output tokens sequentially, has become increasingly important with the widespread deployment of LLM-based applications. As inference workloads continue to scale, GPU memory has emerged as a critical bottleneck: the long input prompts and generation sequences common in agentic and reasoning workloads lead to substantial key-value (KV) cache usage. In this paper, we study the resulting online scheduling problem from a queueing perspective. Requests arrive stochastically with heterogeneous prompt and output lengths, undergo prefill and autoregressive decode, and compete for a finite KV-cache capacity. Unlike classical queueing models, the duration of a processing step depends on both prefill computation and KV-cache I/O, so service capacity is jointly determined by computation, memory access, and memory occupancy. We develop a fluid model that reduces the system to a multiclass single-server queue with effective service rates capturing computation, memory access, and memory capacity. This fluid analysis yields a $cμ$ priority rule, where the effective service rate $μ$ is jointly determined by computational speed, memory bandwidth, and memory capacity. We prove that this rule minimizes cumulative holding cost in the fluid model and, for a finite workload, also minimizes completion time and maximizes full-run output-token throughput. We then construct a feasible scheduling policy for the original finite system and prove that its scaled dynamics converge to the optimal fluid policy. Finally, experiments on a real LLM serving engine using an NVIDIA H800 show that practical implementations of the proposed priority rule substantially reduce average latency while maintaining high throughput relative to existing scheduling policies.

Optimization and Control.title: Generic factorizations and alternating direction method for fixed-rank approximation of matrix polynomials
Optimization and Control.summary: We present an algorithm for approximating a given matrix polynomial of degree $d$ by a matrix polynomial of prescribed rank and degree at most $d$. The method builds on recent advances in the theory of generic eigenstructures and factorizations of matrix polynomials with bounded rank and degree. We also give a specialized treatment of the case of matrix pencils (degree one matrix polynomials), motivated by its particular theoretical and practical importance. Lastly, numerical experiments are reported to assess the performance of the proposed approach and to compare it with existing methods.

Optimization and Control.title: Towards European Hydrogen Market Design: Perspectives from Transmission System Operators
Optimization and Control.summary: Despite hydrogen being central to Europe's decarbonisation strategy, only a small share of renewable hydrogen projects reached final investment decision. A key barrier is uncertainty about how future hydrogen markets will be designed and operated, particularly under Renewable Fuels of Non-Biological Origin requirements. This study investigates the extent to which future hydrogen market design can be adapted from existing natural gas markets, and the challenges it must address. The analysis was based on a survey on future hydrogen market design targeting European gas transmission system operators, the stakeholder group responsible for operating the network and implementing the Network Codes. The survey provided an assessment of mechanism transferability and identified challenges for the early development of the hydrogen market. Core market design principles and trading frameworks are broadly transferable from natural gas markets, as entry-exit systems and virtual trading points. Capacity allocation requires targeted adaptation to improve coupling with electricity markets.
